projects.title: OpenFOAM Thermal Verification
projects.summary: I built an automated workflow to check OpenFOAM heat-transfer simulations against analytical solutions and energy balances.
projects.outcome: On the same coarse room model, continuing the run with a stricter stopping rule cut the wall energy imbalance from 7.96% to 0.918%.

media.alt: OpenFOAM results for heat radiated by a slab, heat leaving and stored in a cylinder, and the room’s wall energy balance
media.caption: The public benchmark checks heat radiated by a slab, heat leaving and stored in a cylinder, and the wall energy balance in a room model.
media.license: Project-authored public figure. See upstream OpenFOAM attribution in THIRD_PARTY.md.

sections.title: Why check the energy balance?
sections.text: The workflow checks the mesh, records how the solver converges and compares results with independent calculations. In the room radiation model, the solver met its stopping criteria while the wall energy imbalance still exceeded the study’s 5% tolerance.

sections.title: What changed in the second run
sections.text: The room run resumed from its previous endpoint on the same mesh, with the same number of radiation directions. It used a stricter convergence threshold for enthalpy and allowed more iterations. The wall energy imbalance then fell below 5%. In a separate set of slab benchmarks, all 21 configurations passed their checks.

sections.title: Scope of the benchmark
sections.text: The numerical checks cover the benchmark cases. How the room result changes with mesh size or radiation direction, and how it compares with experiments, remain open questions.

feature_media.alt: Wall heat flows and their net total as the OpenFOAM room run continues
feature_media.caption: Heat flow at the room walls and the net balance over the continued simulation.
feature_media.license: Project-authored public figure. See upstream OpenFOAM attribution in THIRD_PARTY.md.

featured_copy.problem: Checks whether OpenFOAM heat-transfer simulations agree with analytical solutions and conserve energy.
featured_copy.proof: The room case documents a heat imbalance after the solver met its stopping criteria.

projects.title: Scientific ML & surrogate modelling

projects.title: Evidence-Based Scientific Writing Editor
projects.summary: A reusable AI skill that helps researchers structure scientific arguments, organise evidence and revise manuscripts.
projects.outcome: The Editor reviews claims against the supplied results and helps place figures where they support the argument.

sections.title: Review a draft or plan a paper
sections.text: Before suggesting changes, the Editor reads the draft and supporting results. Its public guide sets out 14 rules and gives a confidence level for each.

sections.title: Keep the author in charge of the claim
sections.text: The rules ask Codex to describe what the study observed before suggesting why it happened. They keep uncertainty visible when the mechanism is unclear. The author decides whether a change in meaning is justified. The effect on manuscript quality remains an open question.

projects.title: Distill Scientific Writing Method
projects.summary: An AI-assisted workflow that derives reusable writing principles from scientific publications, with expert commentary where available. It checks proposed rules against supporting evidence and counterexamples.
projects.outcome: Python scripts set up the review files and check that each draft rule includes fields for supporting examples and exceptions.

sections.title: Find patterns across papers
sections.text: The skill helps an analyst compare how authors explain methods, present results and qualify claims. It records what the papers show, what an author says about their choices and what the analyst infers. When examples disagree or the author’s contribution is unclear, the notes record that uncertainty.

sections.title: Turn the notes into a writing guide
sections.text: The skill writes a guide and a table linking each rule to examples and exceptions. A reviewer decides which rules are well supported and where they apply. The companion Editor can use a reviewed guide when working on another manuscript.

sections.title: Check the files before using the guide
sections.text: In a check of the public scripts, the setup script created the expected files and refused to overwrite a populated directory. The checker caught incomplete records. The reviewer still decides whether the examples support the proposed rules.

projects.title: Top-Journal Palette Miner
projects.summary: A browser tool that analyses colours in scientific figures and suggests how to use them in a new chart.
projects.outcome: Inspect a figure and check colour contrast in your browser. Export palette choices as JSON or CSS and save a report from Transfer Lab.

media.alt: Palette Lab Inspect interface showing extracted colour candidates and visual roles for its built-in synthetic figure
media.caption: The Inspect tab shows colour swatches and possible roles for a built-in example.
media.license: Capture of the owner’s public MIT-licensed interface and original synthetic example.

sections.title: Inspect colours in a figure
sections.text: Inspect samples colours from an image in your browser. It shows how common each colour is, suggests roles such as a data series, a neutral or a highlight, and checks contrast against white. Check those suggestions against what the figure is meant to communicate.

sections.title: Try the palette on a new figure
sections.text: Transfer uses the chart type, number of series and what you want to highlight to suggest colours. The built-in example warns that it could not find a clear neutral colour. Review the contrast and emphasis before using the export.

sections.title: Where the examples come from
sections.text: The images on this page are original synthetic examples. The repository also includes separately licensed examples and lists their sources and any changes.

gallery.caption: Three synthetic examples showing different jobs for colour in a figure.

featured_copy.proof: The browser demo shows how to review colour roles and check contrast using sample figures.

projects.title: Career Intelligence Lab
projects.summary: I built a bilingual tool for researchers and engineers to track vacancies, match their experience to requirements and draft applications.
projects.outcome: The public demo shows where a match comes from and which points need checking. The local workspace supports drafting in English and Simplified Chinese.

sections.title: Match experience to the role
sections.text: The tool separates direct and transferable matches from possible matches, gaps and missing information. Each match keeps its source reference in English and Simplified Chinese. New or edited translations stay out of drafts until reviewed.

sections.title: Work with your own records locally
sections.text: The single-user workspace keeps your records on your own machine. You can review each match, its source and the wording before using a draft.

sections.title: What was tested
sections.text: All 14 automated tests passed using fictional data. A browser walkthrough also checked saving, reviewing translations and preparing drafts. Hiring outcomes and multi-user use remain open questions.

media.alt: Career Intelligence Lab demo showing a job requirement, a possible match, its source and a question to check
media.caption: The public demo uses fictional candidate information. Here, it shows a possible match and a question the candidate needs to check.
media.license: Portfolio capture of the owner’s MIT-licensed public demo, using its synthetic fixture.

featured_copy.problem: Helps researchers and engineers match their experience to job requirements and draft applications in English or Simplified Chinese.
featured_copy.proof: The public demo uses fictional data to show where matches come from and which ones need review.

projects.title: Personal Investment Research
projects.summary: A Python research tool for comparing investment plans under the same assumptions, developed after a trading rule performed poorly on historical data.
projects.outcome: The offline tool filters options by the user’s constraints and records cash and holdings so the plan comparison can be checked.

media.alt: Offline comparison of four investment plans using simulated pound prices, with a drawdown check
media.caption: The recorded demo compares four plans using the same simulated prices, deposits and costs.
media.license: Project-authored media under the project’s MIT licence.

sections.title: What the historical test showed
sections.text: I tested a rule for buying stocks after a price drop. The historical simulation made a profit in 2 of 14 complete quarters held out for testing. It lagged a buy-and-hold comparison with matched capital in all 14. The result depends on which stocks were included and how orders were simulated. Data vendors may revise records, some data had already been inspected, and daily prices do not show which price was reached first.

sections.title: Compare plans under the same conditions
sections.text: The offline tool screens a catalogue against the user’s constraints and can return an empty list. Its example compares a 60/40 allocation with holding cash, buying and holding a broad equity investment, and investing in stages. All four use the same simulated prices in pounds, deposits and costs. The example checks the workflow. Its usefulness in real markets remains untested.

sections.title: How I worked with AI on the project
sections.text: I set the research question, asked for a common basis for comparison and kept the poor historical result in the record. ChatGPT and Codex helped find sources, design the tests, write code and check the results. The tool compares assumptions for research and gives no investment recommendation or trade instruction.
